122 THIRTY-THIRD REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
June 30, 1916. 
Mr. Warren J. Brown, Mr. Henry C. Mansfield, and Mrs. Florence E. Cleve￾land may be appointed as clerks in the classified service of the Government with￾out reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recom￾mendation of the Secretary of War, who submits a detailed report from the 
governor of the Panama Canal giving special reasons as to why the same should 
be issued, in view of which it is believed that the appointment of these three 
persons will be in the interest of the service. From the governor’s report it ap￾pears that Messrs. Brown and Mansfield have rendered long and very satisfac￾tory service in the employment of the Government on the Isthmus of Panama; 
and that Mrs. Cleveland, whose husband was killed May 23, 1914, while em￾ployed as an operator of one of the towing locomotives of the Panama Canal, 
has been employed in an excepted position in the Panama Canal service since 
November 16, 1914, in which position it appears she has rendered very satis￾factory service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Mrs. Olivia Blanchard may be appointed to a position in the classified service 
under the Department of Labor without reference to the civil-service rules. This 
order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Labor, who states 
that the department contemplates the establishment of a branch of the United 
States Employment Service in the city of New Orleans, La., and that it is neces￾sary that a woman employee be assigned thereto to attend to applications of 
women for employment or help, and it is believed that a woman as favorably 
known in New Orleans as Mrs. Blanchard is would possess advantages calcu￾lated to promote the interests of the new employment service, and that her 
acquaintance would make her services desirable in the labors of woman’s and 
girl’s division of said service involving vocational direction as to industrial 
training of girls. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Mr. Marion T. Edwards may be appointed to the position of assistant messen￾ger qualified in the operation and repair of automobiles, in the Bureau of Stand￾ards at $720 per annum, without reference to the civil-service rules. This order 
is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of Commerce and the Direc￾tor of the Bureau of Standards, who state that the position to which it is pro￾posed to appoint Mr. Edwards is a confidential post; that by experience and 
training Mr. Edwards is especially qualified for the position; and that his ap￾pointment would be in the interests of good administration. The Civil Service 
Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
July 14, 1916. 
Miss Ruth L. O'Donnell may be appointed to a position in the Bureau of Effi￾ciency without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the 
recommendation of the Chief of the Bureau of Efficiency, who states that Miss 
O’Donnell has been employed in his office at various times during the past two 
years; that her services have been most satisfactory; and that her permanent 
appointment to the force of the Bureau of Efficiency would be a distinct advan￾tage to the bureau. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recom￾mendation. 
July 18, 1916. 
Mr. Jacob P. Smith may be appointed a storekeeper-gauger in the Internal￾Revenue Service without compliance with civil-service rules. The collector of 
internal revenue for the seventh district of Indiana states that Mr. Smith served 
temporarily as a storekeeper-gauger in that district from September, 1915, until 
June 26, 1916; that he is qualified to competently fill any position in the store￾keeper-gauger service; and that his permanent appointment will be in the inter￾est of efficient administration. The collector further states that the stress of 
work at this time in his district necessitates the employment of an experienced 
man. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treas￾ury. Mr. Smith is on the civil-service register. 
July 19, 1916. 
Mr, Arthur E. Wilson may be permanently appointed to a clerical position in 
the office of the Surgeon General, Public Health Service, without reference to

Mrs. Alexander Walters may be appointed to a position in the Immigration

August 2, 1916. 
The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit 
the reinstatement of Ernest Szemelenyi as a clerk at $1,200 per annum in the 
Patent Office. Mr. Szemelenyi served from 1881 to 1909 as a translator in the 
Patent Office. The Commissioner of Patents, who has been personally cogni￾zant of the character of his work for 20 years, states that his acquaintance 
with foreign languages and the practical arts and science combined gives him 
a range of ability for handling certain business of the Patent Office which is 
unique; that no one has ever been able to distribute foreign patents among 
the different divisions as acceptably as Mr. Szemelenyi did while he was so 
employed ; and that he desires to have the appointment authorized by Execu￾tive order because of the needs of the office and because it is impossible to get

office can pay. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the Secretary of 
the Interior in recommending this Executive order. 
August 8, 1916. 
The year limit on eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit 
the reinstatement of Mr, Arthur 8. Hull as a fourth assistant examiner in the Patent Office. In view of Mr. Hull's efficient service as an examiner and his

of the continuing difficulty of obtaining a sufficient number of qualified eligibles

the recommendation. 
August 10, 1916. 
Mrs. Myrtle M. Davis, of Arkansas, may be appointed in the postal service 
without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service 
rules. This order is issued at the suggestion of the Postmaster General, the 
husband of Mrs. Davis having been assassinated while in the actual perform￾ance of his duties as a rural carrier on route No. 3 from England, Ark. 
August 31, 1916. 
Mr. Henry Braxton may be promoted from the grade of messenger to a clerk￾ship in the Treasury Department without compliance with the requirements 
of the Civil Service Commission relative to examinations. This order is issued 
upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that 
Mr. Braxton served as messenger in the office of the commissioner of railroads 
from 1892 to 1899, when he was transferred to the Treasury Department, where 
he has since served most efficiently in the offices of the Secretary of the Treas￾ury and the Comptroller of the Currency, rendering very valuable service, and 
that it is believed his promotion will be in the interest of the service. The 
Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

122 THIRTY-FOURTH REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
December 20, 1916. 
Mr. William C. Rader may be appointed Assistant to the Director of the Bureau of War Risk Insurance in the Treasury Department without compliance with civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that the position of Assistant to the Director of the Bureau of War Risk Insurance is a technical one; that there is no person.in the Treasury Department qualified to fill the position, and that Mr. Rader possesses the necessary qualifications, and that his 
appointment will be in the interest of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
December 28, 1916. 
Miss Anne M. Roden may be permanently appointed in the classified service of the Treasury Department without compliance with the civil-service requirements. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who 
states that Miss Roden is temporarily employed, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, in the office of the Auditor for the War Department, where her services have proven most valuable as a calculating machine operator, and it is be- lieved that her permanent appointment will be greatly in the interest of the service. 
January 3, 1917. 
Mr. Dolley Farrior may be appointed to a position as messenger, or to any position in which his services can be utilized, under the War Department, without regard to the requirements of the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of War, who states that Mr. Farrior was troop quartermaster sergeant of Troop C, Tenth Cavalry; that he was wounded in the right wrist in action at Carrizal, Mexico, June 21, 1916, as a result of which his right hand is paralyzed, the bullet having severed the nerve; that he was discharged on surgeon’s certificate of disability, October 31, 1916, with character “Excellent’’; and that he is reported to be a trustworthy man as shown by his being troop quartermaster sergeant, a position involving responsibility under the captain for all the property of the troop. 
January 5, 1917. 
Mr. Frank Kearney may be promoted from the position of messenger to the $1,000 clerical grade in the classified service of the Treasury Department. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Kearney is a hard working, faithful and efficient employee, who has given more than 35 years’ service to the Government, and that on July 19, 1911, while in the per- formance of his official duties and without negligence on his part, he received injuries from which he will never recover; yet he performs all his duties most capably; that 
there is a vacancy in the $1,000 clerical grade in the office of the Comptroller of the Treasury for which Mr. Kearney is in every way qualified because of his long experi- ence in that office, and it is believed that his promotion to this grade will be in the interests of the service. 
January 19, 191%. 
Mr. Austin F. Hawes may be reinstated as extension specialist in forestry at a salary of $2,760 per annum in the States Relations Service of the Department of Agriculture without regard to the year limit of the reinstatement rule. Mr. Hawes was appointed a forest assistant in 1903 through examination under the civil-service rules, and served until 1906, when he became State forester of Con- necticut. In 1909 he became State forester of Vermont and professor of forestry at the University of Vermont. The Department of Agriculture states that it is believed that his reinstatement would be in the interests of good administration. The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order. 
January 25, 1917. 
Mr. Michael Flaherty may be promoted to a subclerical position or to the position of wireman in the Treasury Department without compliance with the requirements of the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Flaherty has been employed as an unclassified laborer in the electrician’s office for the last four years and has made himself particularly valuable in that office, and that it is believed his promotion to a classified position will be in the interests of the service. : The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation.

EXCEPTIONS FROM EXAMINATION. 128 
February 14, 1917. : 
Mrs. Nora A. Fennell may be reinstated as an operative in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing without regard to the length of time she has been separated from the service. Mrs. Fennell served as a printer’s assistant and operative in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing continuously from March 12, 1900, to April 16, 1903, when she resigned“to be married. It appears from the statement of the Secretary of the Treasury that Mrs. Fennell is a widow with three children dependent upon her for support, and that she is still a young woman in excellent health and capable of ren- dering in the future, as she rendered in the past, efficient service. The register of eligibles for original appointment to the position of printer’s assistant is practically exhausted, for which reason and in view of the other facts above an the com- mission, concurs with the Secretary of the Treasury in a recommendation for an Execu- ' tive order. : 
February 17, 1917. 
Mrs. Mary R. Livingston Stephenson may be appointed to a position as skilled laborer in the Government Printing Office without reference to the civil-service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Public Printer, who states that Mrs. Stephenson is the widow of John K. Stephenson, a former employee of the Government Printing Office who was a very conscientious and earnest worker, and that through his efforts several formulas were adopted for the manufacture of certain kinds of printing inks which are now in use in that office. He further states that the services of Mrs. Stephenson can be utilized to advantage as a skilled laborer. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
February 21, 1917. 
Mr. John E. Amis may be appointed to a clerical position in any executive depart- ment or independent office, without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Amis has been employed since September 3, 1915, as office deputy marshal in the office of the United States marshal at Nashville, Tenn., having been appointed without examination as the position is excepted from examination by authority of law. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order. 
March 13, 1917. 
Isaac Bassett, Thomas Harkness, and William H. Wise, guides at the Washington Navy Yard, may be appointed as watchmen in that yard without examination under the civil-service rules. These men, although not employees of the Government, have served for

EXCEPTION OF CERTAIN POSITIONS IN NAVAL ACADEMY. 
February 27, 1917. ; 
Schedule A, Subdivision V, paragraph 2, of the civil-service rules, which at present excepts from examination civilian professors, instructors, and teachers in the Naval Academy, is hereby amended to read as follows: ¢“2. In the United States Naval Academy: ‘‘(a) Professors, instructors, and teachers. 
“(b) Baker helpers, coffeemen, firemen, linenman, pantrymen, dish pantrymen, scullions, utility men, waiters, and, when promoted from the position of waiter, head and assistant head waiter.” 
The Navy Department recommended that these positions be excepted from exami- nation for the reasons that the salaries are low; that the positions have been filled from waiters, formerly paid from the mess fund, who have shown themselves trust- worthy; that practically no education is required, and that the requisite knowledge can only be acquired by actual experience in the commissary. The commission recommended the order. 
ALL POSITIONS OF STOREKEEPER AND GAUGER, INTERNAL-REVENUE SERVICE, MADE 
COMPETITIVE. 
February 21, 1917. 
Schedule A, excepting from examination certain positions under the civil-service rules, is hereby amended by striking out paragraph 4 of Subdivision III, Treasury 
Department, which reads as follows: ‘4. Storekeepers and gaugers whose compensation does not exceed $3 per diem when actually employed and whose aggregate compensation shall not exceed $500 per annum. “This exception from the requirement of examination shall not apply to the fifth internal-revenue district of North Carolina.” 
This order was recommended by the commission in view of the decision of the Treasury Department to make no further appointments under this provision of the rules. The department’s reasons for this action are shown in the following quotation from Treasury Decision 2438: 
“It has been brought to the attention of this office that a too fine division of duties imposed upon internal-revenue officers, such as storekeepers, storekeeper-gaugers, etc., assigned to distilleries has resulted in limiting the work performed by said officers and for that reason an excessive number is frequently assigned to duty, whereas with a notice of assignment of a broader character it would appear that a less number of officers in many cases could easily perform all necessary services under the direction of collectors. “With a view to correcting this condition the Secretary of the Treasury will be requested to change the designations of all officers now in commission as storekeepers or as gaugers to storekeeper-gaugers. When this action is taken and new commissions are issued, collectors will be notified and the officers will be required to furnish bonds as storekeeper-gaugers. In the event that any officers refuse to file new bonds report should be made to that effect. No officer who refuses to qualify by giving bond under the changed designation will be assigned to duty, and collectors will not recommend such assignments after opportunity has been afforded for such qualifications. ‘After the receipt hereof collectors will not recommend for assignment storekeeper- gaugers appointed under civil-service rule 2, section 3, Schedule A, and hereafter no more storekeeper-gaugers will be appointed under said rule.”

June 12, 1917. 
Schedule A, Section XI, of positions excepted from the requirement of examination under ihe civil-service rules, is hereby amended by the addition of the following aragraph: ’ «“q, tent assistants in the Bureau of Standards whose salary shall not exceed arate of $300 a year each while employed, provided that no person shall be eligible for appointment as student assistant who is not a bona fide student pursuing a technical or scientific course at a high school or college of recognized standing. Appointments under this section shall not continue for a os period than six months in any one year, except upon prior approval of the commission and then only in exceptionally meritorious cases. the summer months at a time when many permanent employees of the bureau are on leave of absence. May 9, 1917. 
Henry S. Grogan, of Minnesota, may be reinstated as a post-office inspector without regard to the year limitation prescribed by Civil Service Rule IX. This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General because of Mr. Grogan’s long and efficient service in various branches of the Postal Service, including 11 years as a letter carrier and subsequent service from 1906 to 1912 as posto-flice inspector, superintendent of station, and assistant superintendent of mails. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation of the Postmaster General for an Executive order.

June 20, 1917. 
Mr. John J. Crowley may be appointed Assistant to the Director of the Bureau of War-Risk Insurance in the Treasury Department, without regard to civil-service requirements. : This order is issued on the recommendation of the Secretary of the Treasury, who states that Mr. Crowley is a life and accident insurance expert and that his services are necessary in connection with the new branch of the Bureau of War-Risk Insurance which has to do with the insurance of masters, officers, and crews of American mer- chant vessels against loss of life or personal injury by the risks of war. 
June 20, 1917. : 
Mr. Charles H. Kesler may be reinstated as an assistant examiner in the Patent 
Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the length of time he has been separated from the service. r. Kesler was appointed an assistant examiner through examination on July 1, 1911, and served until September 13, 1915, when he resigned. After his resignation he was engaged in work in the office of a patent attorney. The Secretary of the Interior recommends the reinstatement as distinctly in the interest of good adminis- tration in view of Mr. Kesler’s satisfactory service and an experience of nearly six years in patent matters. The Civil Service Commission concurs in recommending this order in view of the foregoing statement and the fact that the number of eligibles for the position of assistant examiner is hardly equal to the demand. 
June 28, 1917. 
Mr. H. H. Chapman may be reinstated as assistant district forester under the Department of Agriculture without regard to the year limitation upon eligibility for reinstatement. Mr. Chapman worked as a student assistant in the Forest Service as early as 1899. In July, 1904, he was appointed forest assistant through appropriate examination, and continued in this position until 1906, when he was appointed instructor in the

Yale Forest School, and the following year became an assistant professor. At various intervals or during summer vacations between 1906 and 1910 he was employed by the department as a collaborator. His resignation from the Forest Service was effected in February, 1914. Since his separation from the service, his work has been along lines tending to enhance his value to the Government. He is considered one of the best foresters in the country, and in the opinion of the department the best interests of the service will be met by his reemployment. The commission concurs in recommending the order. 
July 5, 1917. 
Mr. J. M. Shaffer may be appointed to a classified position in the Treasury Depart- ment without reference to civil-service rules. This order is issued on the recom- mendation of the Secretary of the Treasury who states that Mr. Shaffer has been temporarily employed in the Treasury Department on a contract basis in connection with the liberty loan, and that his services have proved so valuable that his perma- nent appointment will be greatly in the interests of the service. Mr. Shaffer was formerly employed in the Department of Agriculture as a result of a civil-service examination, and served there from August, 1913, to August, 1916, at which time he resigned. He is eligible for reinstatement in that department, but under the civil-service rules would have to serve there six months before he would be eligible for transfer to the Treasury Department. 
July 6, 1917. 
Mrs. Mary C. Ritenour, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service at a salary not to exceed $900 per annum without regard to the civil-service rules. Mrs. Ritenour was appointed as a printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Engraving
